Author

About this section

Section 02 is still foundational C++, but it’s where C++ stops looking like Python. It covers what Python hides from you:

  • One name, many types. Chapter 05 lets several functions share a name (overloading), and Chapter 06 lets the compiler write the functions for us (templates).
  • Referring to objects. Chapter 07 introduces value categories and references, and with them pass by reference. Chapter 08 introduces pointers and pass by address. Python has only something that feels similar: passing an immutable object behaves a bit like pass by value, and passing a mutable object a bit like pass by reference.
  • Memory you manage yourself. Chapter 09 creates objects while the program runs, on the heap, and shows how to give that memory back.

The notes work as in Section 01: each chapter matches the slide deck with the same number, the name above a listing is a file in that chapter’s cpp/ folder, and the coloured boxes mark Python comparisons (blue), key ideas (navy), best practices (green) and common mistakes (amber).

5 Function Overloading and Default Arguments

This chapter lets several functions share one name, shows how the compiler decides which one a call means, and lets a function fill in arguments the caller leaves out.

5.1 Function overloading

int add(int x, int y) adds two integers, but it’s no good for two doubles: the arguments would be converted to int, losing their fractional parts. Giving every version its own name, add_integer, add_double and so on, quickly gets out of hand once you add add(int, double), add(double, int) or three numbers. Function overloading lets several functions share one name, as long as their parameter types differ. Each one is an overloaded function, or overload.

function_overloading.cpp
#include <iostream>

int add(int x, int y) { // integer version
    return x + y;
}

double add(double x, double y) { // floating-point version
    return x + y;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << add(1, 2) << '\n';        // add(int, int)
    std::cout << add(42.25, 24.5) << '\n'; // add(double, double)
    return 0;
}

3
66.75

You write add every time, and the compiler works out which add you mean from the arguments. Matching a call to the right overload is called overload resolution:

overload_resolution.cpp
#include <iostream>

int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }
double add(double x, double y) { return x + y; }
double add(double x, double y, double z) { return x + y + z; }

int main() {
    std::cout << add(1, 2) << '\n';     // add(int, int)
    std::cout << add(1.2, 3.4) << '\n'; // add(double, double)

    // add(double, double, double): 1 (an int) and 2.5f (a float)
    // both become doubles
    std::cout << add(1, 2.5f, 1.2) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

3
4.6
4.7

The third call has three arguments, so only the three-parameter version fits, and its int and float arguments are converted to double.

NoteComing from Python

Python has no overloading: a second def add simply replaces the first. In C++, both exist side by side.

A program with overloads compiles only if every overload can be told apart from the others, and every call can be resolved to exactly one of them. It’s common sense: if you can’t tell which function is meant, neither can the compiler.

5.2 Telling overloads apart

Overloads can differ in the number of parameters, or in their types:

int add(int x, int y);
int add(int x, int y, int z);   // a different number of parameters
double add(double x, double y); // different types
double add(int x, double y);    // different types

Two things do not tell overloads apart. The first is a type alias, a second name for an existing type: using Age = int; (or the older typedef int Age;) makes print(Age) exactly the same as print(int). Likewise, const on a value parameter doesn’t count. The second is the return type:

int get_random_value();
double get_random_value(); // error: ambiguating new declaration

Imagine you’re the compiler and you meet the call get_random_value(). Which one would you call? The call gives you no clue, so C++ doesn’t allow it.

The parts of a function that tell overloads apart are its signature: its name plus the number and types of its parameters. So int add(int x, int y) has the signature add(int, int). The return type and the parameter names are not part of it, and every overload must have a different signature.

5.3 How the compiler picks an overload

Overload resolution takes three steps:

  1. Candidates: every function with that name.
  2. Viable functions: the candidates with the right number of parameters, where each argument can be converted to the parameter’s type.
  3. Best match: an exact match beats a promotion (such as float to double), which beats any other conversion. If one function is strictly better than all the others, it’s called.

If two overloads are equally good, the compiler refuses to guess:

ambiguous_match.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print(int x) { std::cout << "int " << x << '\n'; }
void print(double x) { std::cout << "double " << x << '\n'; }

int main() {
    print(5);   // exact match: print(int)
    print(5.0); // exact match: print(double)
    print(5L);  // a long: converts to int AND to double. Which?
    return 0;
}

error: call of overloaded 'print(long int)' is ambiguous

5L is a long, and converting it to int or to double is equally good, so neither wins. The fix is to pass an argument of the type you mean, such as 5 or 5.0.

5.3.1 Deleting unwanted calls with = delete

Conversions can also make calls work that shouldn’t. Given only void print_int(int x), the call print_int('a') prints 97 (the number that stores 'a') and print_int(true) prints 1, because char and bool both convert silently to int (print_int_surprise.cpp). If that makes no sense for your function, forbid it:

delete_function.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print_int(int x) { std::cout << x << '\n'; }

void print_int(char) = delete; // calling these is now an error
void print_int(bool) = delete;

int main() {
    print_int(97);  // fine
    print_int('a'); // error: use of deleted function
    return 0;
}

error: use of deleted function 'void print_int(char)'

= delete declares an overload that must not be called. Overload resolution still picks it for a char argument, and the compiler then reports an error. Careful: print_int(5.0) is now an error too, because a double converts equally well to int, char and bool, so the call is ambiguous.

5.4 Default arguments

A default argument is a value a parameter gets when the caller doesn’t supply one:

default_argument.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print(int x, int y = 4) { // 4 is the default argument
    std::cout << "x: " << x << ", y: " << y << '\n';
}

int main() {
    print(1, 2); // y uses the argument we give: 2
    print(3);    // y uses the default: same as print(3, 4)
    return 0;
}

x: 1, y: 2
x: 3, y: 4

With several defaults, arguments are matched to parameters from the left, and the defaults fill in the rest from the right:

multiple_default_arguments.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print_numbers(int x = 10, int y = 20, int z = 30) {
    std::cout << x << ' ' << y << ' ' << z << '\n';
}

int main() {
    print_numbers(1, 2, 3); // no defaults used
    print_numbers(1, 2);    // z defaulted
    print_numbers(1);       // y and z defaulted
    print_numbers();        // all three defaulted
    return 0;
}

1 2 3
1 2 30
1 20 30
10 20 30

C++ has no syntax like print_numbers( , , 3), and the rules follow from that. You can’t skip an argument: to give z a value, you must also give x and y. Defaults must come last: once a parameter has a default, every parameter to its right needs one too, so void print(int x = 10, int y); is an error. And among the defaulted parameters, put the one callers change most often first.

NoteComing from Python

Python lets you name arguments in a call: print_numbers(z=3). C++ has no named arguments, so the order of parameters matters much more.

5.4.1 Where the default goes

A function with a forward declaration can have its default in the declaration or in the definition, but not both: repeating it gives error: default argument given for parameter 2 (default_argument_twice.cpp). And because the compiler reads from top to bottom, it must see the default before the call; if the default is only in a definition below main(), the call print(3) fails with too few arguments (default_argument_too_late.cpp). So put the default in the forward declaration, which in a multi-file program means the header:

print.h
#ifndef PRINT_H
#define PRINT_H

void print(int x, int y = 4); // default

#endif

print.cpp defines print(int x, int y) without repeating the default, and main.cpp, which includes print.h, can call print(5) to print x: 5, y: 4.

TipBest practice

Give a default in the forward declaration if there is one (especially in a header), otherwise in the definition.

5.4.2 Default arguments and overloading

Functions with default arguments can be overloaded: with print(std::string) and print(char c = '*'), the call print() prints * (default_argument_overloaded.cpp). But a default is not part of the signature, so it can make a call match two overloads:

default_argument_ambiguous.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print(int x) { std::cout << x << '\n'; }
void print(int x, int y = 10) { std::cout << x << ' ' << y << '\n'; }

int main() {
    print(1, 2); // fine: only print(int, int) takes two arguments
    print(1);    // error: print(int) or print(int, int = 10)?
    return 0;
}

error: call of overloaded 'print(int)' is ambiguous

5.5 Summary

  • Overloading: functions can share a name if their signatures (name, number and types of parameters) differ. The return type doesn’t count.
  • Overload resolution picks the best match; an exact match beats a conversion. If two overloads tie, the call is ambiguous and won’t compile.
  • = delete forbids particular calls.
  • Default arguments fill in parameters the caller leaves out. Defaults must be the rightmost parameters, and can’t be skipped.
  • Give a default once, in the forward declaration (header) if there is one, and before it’s used. Defaults are not part of the signature, so they can make calls ambiguous.

Further reading on learncpp.com: overload resolution and ambiguous matches (the full ranking rules are long: try asking Gemini to teach them to you), implicit type conversion, type aliases.

6 Function Templates

Overloading means writing every version of a function by hand. This chapter lets the compiler write them for us, from one function template.

6.1 Why templates?

You’ve already used templates in the labs. std::vector<double> is a growable list of doubles, and std::vector<int> the same thing holding ints. std::max(1, 2) works out that both arguments are int, while std::max<double>(10, 42.24) tells it to treat both as double. The type in angle brackets < > picks the type: std::vector and std::max are templates, written once and usable with many types.

Without templates, a max() function needs one overload per type:

int max(int x, int y) {
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

double max(double x, double y) { // the same code again
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

c ? a : b is the conditional operator: “if c then a, otherwise b”, like Python’s a if c else b. Two copies of the same code already, and every new type (long, float, char…) means another. What we’d like is to write T max(T x, T y) once, where T stands for any type for which x < y makes sense. A template gives us exactly that: one definition with a placeholder type, from which the compiler generates a real function for each type we actually use.

6.2 Writing and using a function template

template <typename T> // the template parameter declaration
T max(T x, T y) {     // the function template itself
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

The template parameter declaration starts with the keyword template and lists the placeholder types in angle brackets. typename T declares T as a type template parameter (class T also works, but typename is preferred). Use T, then U, V… when the meaning is obvious, and a descriptive name starting with a capital letter, like Allocator, when the parameter has a specific job. To use the template, put the actual type, the template argument, in angle brackets:

use_template_function.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T max(T x, T y) {
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << max<int>(1, 2) << '\n';        // instantiates max<int>
    std::cout << max<double>(1.5, 0.5) << '\n'; // instantiates max<double>
    return 0;
}

2
1.5

6.2.1 Instantiation

Creating a real function from a template is called instantiation, and it happens when a call needs it (implicit instantiation). For max<int>(1, 2), the compiler copies the template, replaces every T with int, and compiles the result, as if we had written:

template <>
int max<int>(int x, int y) { // generated for T = int
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

(The template <> line marks it as generated from the template; you won’t write this yourself, but instantiation_look_breakdown.cpp shows it compiles.) The generated function is a function instance, an ordinary function in every way, and the template it came from is the primary template. A template is instantiated the first time a call needs a type, and later calls with that type reuse the same instance: in instantiation_look_more.cpp, two calls to max<int> and one to max<double> produce just two functions. A template that is never called produces no function at all.

ImportantKey idea

A function template is not a function. It’s a recipe for making functions.

6.3 Template argument deduction

The template argument usually just repeats the types of the arguments: in max<int>(1, 2), 1 and 2 are ints anyway. So we can leave it out and let the compiler deduce T from the arguments. max<>(1, 2) deduces T and considers only templates; max(1, 2) deduces T and considers ordinary functions too. The second form looks like an ordinary call, and it’s the one we normally use. But note what happens when an ordinary function matches equally well:

template_argument_deduction_more.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T max(T x, T y) {
    std::cout << "template max<T>: ";
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

int max(int x, int y) {
    std::cout << "ordinary max: ";
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << max<int>(1, 2) << '\n'; // template, T = int
    std::cout << max<>(1, 2) << '\n';    // template, T deduced
    std::cout << max(1, 2) << '\n';      // ordinary wins
    return 0;
}

template max<T>: 2
template max<T>: 2
ordinary max: 2
ImportantKey idea

When an ordinary function and a template instance match equally well, max(1, 2) picks the ordinary function.

That’s useful. In favor_normal_func_over_func_template_call.cpp, a template print(T x) handles every type in a general way, and an ordinary print(bool x) prints true or false instead of 1 or 0. With the normal call print(true), the special version wins automatically.

TipBest practice

Call function templates with the normal syntax, print(true), unless you specifically need the template version.

6.4 What templates can and can’t do

A function template can mix template parameters with ordinary ones, which can have default arguments: template <typename T> void print_repeated(T value, int times = 1) prints any value times times (func_template_with_non_template_parameters.cpp).

The template itself is only checked properly once it’s instantiated, and some instances don’t compile:

instantiated_func_not_compile.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

template <typename T>
T add_value(T x, double v) {
    return x + v;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << add_value(4.2, 2.4) << '\n'; // fine: double + double

    std::string hello{"Hello, world!"};
    std::cout << add_value(hello, 4.2) << '\n'; // string + double?!
    return 0;
}

error: no match for 'operator+' (operand types are 'std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>' and 'double')

…followed by dozens of lines of notes. The template is fine, but the instance add_value<std::string> isn’t, because you can’t add a double to a string. Template error messages are famously long: read the first line first. Worse, some instances compile but make no sense:

not_make_sense_semantically.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T add_one(T x) {
    return x + 1;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << add_one(41) << '\n';              // fine: 42
    std::cout << add_one("Hello, world!") << '\n'; // compiles... but?
    return 0;
}

42
ello, world!

"Hello, world!" is not a std::string but a C-style string, so T becomes the memory address of its first character. Adding 1 moves on to the next character, and the H is lost. (Addresses are Chapter 08’s topic.) The compiler can’t know that wasn’t what you meant.

6.4.1 Templates live in header files

max.h
#ifndef MAX_H
#define MAX_H

// The whole template lives here
template <typename T>
T max(T x, T y) {
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

#endif

To instantiate max<int>, the compiler needs the template’s whole definition, body included, in every .cpp file that uses it; a declaration alone isn’t enough. So templates go entirely in the header, and they are exempt from the “define exactly once” rule. This is the exception to the header rules from Chapter 02.

6.5 Templates with several types

max(2, 3.5) doesn’t compile:

error: no matching function for call to 'max(int, double)'
note:   deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')

T can only be one type: from 2 the compiler deduces int, from 3.5 it deduces double, and it refuses to choose. One fix is to say which type you want, max<double>(2, 3.5): there’s nothing left to deduce, and 2 is simply converted to 2.0. It would be nicer not to have to think about the types at all, though. So let x and y have different types:

two_template_type_parameters.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T, typename U> // two type template parameters
T max(T x, U y) {                 // x has type T, y has type U
    return (x < y) ? y : x;       // the result is converted to T!
}

int main() {
    std::cout << max(2, 3.5) << '\n'; // T = int, U = double
    return 0;
}

3

Why 3, not 3.5? The return type is T, which is int, so the result 3.5 is converted to int. No error, no warning: just a wrong answer. The fix is to let the compiler work out the return type from the return statement, with auto: template <typename T, typename U> auto max(T x, U y) returns a double here, and prints 3.5. (Alternatively, std::common_type_t<T, U> from <type_traits> names the type that both T and U convert to without losing information, such as double for int and double; but auto is usually simpler.)

auto works for variables too: it asks the compiler to deduce a type from the initializer.

auto age{25};                    // int
auto price{42.99};               // double
auto name{std::string{"Khiem"}}; // std::string

This does not make C++ dynamically typed like Python: each variable still gets exactly one type, fixed at compile time; you just don’t have to spell it out. Careful: plain auto drops const, so write const auto to keep it.

6.5.1 Abbreviated function templates (C++20)

Since C++20, a parameter of type auto turns an ordinary function into a function template, with one type template parameter per auto:

abbreviated_function_template.cpp
#include <iostream>

auto max(auto x, auto y) { // C++20: a template without the template line
    return (x < y) ? y : x;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << max(2, 3.5) << '\n';   // int and double
    std::cout << max('a', 'z') << '\n'; // char and char
    return 0;
}

3.5
z

This is shorthand for template <typename T, typename U> auto max(T x, U y). Function templates can also be overloaded like ordinary functions, for example with two and three parameters (function_templates_overloaded.cpp).

6.6 Non-type template parameters

Remember constexpr variables from Chapter 04? A function can be constexpr too, so that the compiler can call it while compiling: with constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }, the value of constexpr int result{square(10)}; is worked out at compile time.

A template parameter doesn’t have to be a type. A non-type template parameter has a fixed type and stands for a value known at compile time: an integer type such as int, char or bool, a floating-point type (since C++20), and a few others we meet later.

nontype_template_parameters.cpp
#include <iostream>

// Factor is a value, not a type
template <int Factor, typename T>
T scale_sensor_reading(T raw_value) {
    return raw_value * Factor;
}

int main() {
    int raw_input{10};

    int high{scale_sensor_reading<5>(raw_input)}; // Factor = 5
    int low{scale_sensor_reading<2>(raw_input)};  // Factor = 2

    std::cout << "Raw: " << raw_input << '\n';
    std::cout << "High (x5): " << high << '\n';
    std::cout << "Low  (x2): " << low << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Raw: 10
High (x5): 50
Low  (x2): 20

Factor is given explicitly in the angle brackets, while T is still deduced from the argument. Each different Factor produces a different function with the value baked in: here, one that multiplies by 5 and one that multiplies by 2 (nontype_template_parameters_pov.cpp shows both).

6.7 Summary

  • A function template is a recipe for functions: template <typename T> introduces a placeholder type T.
  • The compiler instantiates a real function for each type a call needs. The template itself is not a function.
  • Template argument deduction works out T from the arguments: write max(1, 2), not max<int>(1, 2). An equally good ordinary function wins.
  • An instance may fail to compile, or compile and do something silly: the compiler only checks it once it’s instantiated.
  • Templates live entirely in header files.
  • For mixed types, use two type parameters with an auto return type, or the C++20 shorthand auto max(auto x, auto y).
  • A non-type template parameter is a compile-time value, like template <int Factor>.

Further reading on learncpp.com: templates with multiple template types, non-type template parameters, type deduction with auto, constexpr functions.

7 Compound Types and References

This chapter introduces references: second names for existing objects. To understand them, we first need value categories. References then give us pass by reference, the way to hand a function an object without copying it.

7.1 Compound types

A program that tracks a hundred employees can’t have a separate int id1, int id2, double salary1… for each one. We need types built from other types: compound types. Some are built into the language: functions (Chapter 02), references (this chapter), pointers (Chapter 08) and C-style arrays. Others are defined by you, the programmer: enumerations, structs, unions, and classes, the heart of this course from Chapter 10. We won’t cover them all; structs and classes are so similar that studying one carefully is enough. Even a function has a compound type: void do_something(int x, double y) has the type void(int, double).

7.2 Value categories: lvalues and rvalues

Every expression has a type, the type of the value it produces (12 / 4 is an int, 12.0 / 4 a double), and a value category, which says what kind of thing it produces: an object, or just a value. Why is x = 5 fine, but 5 = x isn’t? The compiler’s answer is in its error message:

lvalue_assignment.cpp
int main() {
    int x{};
    x = 5; // fine: x is a variable we can assign to
    5 = x; // error: you can't assign to 5
    return 0;
}

error: lvalue required as left operand of assignment

  • An lvalue evaluates to an identifiable object (or function): something with a name or an address, which outlives the expression. A variable x is an lvalue.
  • An rvalue evaluates to a value: a literal, a temporary result, something returned by value. It’s gone at the end of the expression.

(C++11 added glvalues, prvalues and xvalues, for a feature called move semantics; lvalues and rvalues are enough for us.) In rvalue_expression_example.cpp, return5(), x + 1 and static_cast<int>(d) all produce temporary values, so they’re rvalues. (static_cast<int>(d) is an explicit conversion: it turns the double 1.2 into the int 1.) One surprise: a string literal like "Hello" is an lvalue, because it’s stored in memory for the whole program. Running the expressions through a small tool, tell_value_categories.cpp, confirms it:

5 is an rvalue
get_int() is an rvalue
x is an lvalue
x + 1 is an rvalue
std::string{"Hello"} is an rvalue
"Hello" is an lvalue
++x is an lvalue
x++ is an rvalue

Operators expect rvalues as operands unless stated otherwise, yet x = y and x = x + 1 compile. Where an rvalue is expected and an lvalue is given, the lvalue goes through an lvalue-to-rvalue conversion: it’s simply evaluated to produce its value. In x = x + 1, the left x is the object we assign to; the right x is converted to its value, say 42, and x + 1 produces the rvalue 43.

ImportantKey idea

An lvalue can be used wherever an rvalue is expected. An rvalue can never be used where an lvalue is required.

7.3 lvalue references

A reference is an alias: a second name for an object that already exists. Anything you do to the reference happens to the object. int& (one ampersand) is an lvalue reference to an int, and const int& an lvalue reference to a const int. (C++11 also added rvalue references, int&&, which many experienced programmers have never needed.) Since lvalue references are by far the most common, “reference” on its own means lvalue reference.

modify_value_through_nonconst_reference.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int x{42};
    int& ref{x}; // ref is another name for x

    std::cout << x << ' ' << ref << '\n';

    x = 24; // change x...
    std::cout << x << ' ' << ref << '\n';

    ref = 12; // ...or change it through ref
    std::cout << x << ' ' << ref << '\n';
    return 0;
}

42 42
24 24
12 12

One object, two names: changing x changes ref, and changing ref changes x.

TipBest practice

Write the ampersand next to the type, int& ref, not next to the name. It’s part of the type.

7.3.1 The rules of references

A reference must be initialized (int& invalid_ref; is an error). Initializing it binds it to an object, its referent. A non-const reference can only bind to a modifiable lvalue:

nonconst_reference_binding.cpp
int main() {
    int x{5};
    int& ref{x}; // fine: x is a modifiable lvalue

    const int y{5};
    int& invalid_ref{y}; // error: y is const

    int& invalid_ref2{0}; // error: 0 is an rvalue
    return 0;
}

error: binding reference of type 'int&' to 'const int' discards qualifiers
error: cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type 'int&' to an rvalue of type 'int'

A non-const reference lets you change its referent, so binding one to a const object, or to a temporary value like 0, would let you change something that must not, or cannot, change. Once bound, a reference can’t be reseated:

reference_cannot_be_reseated.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int x{5};
    int y{6};

    int& ref{x}; // ref is another name for x

    ref = y; // does this make ref refer to y?

    std::cout << x << '\n'; // what does this print?
    return 0;
}

This prints 6. ref = y does not make ref refer to y: ref is x, so this is simply x = y. (A Python name, by contrast, can be rebound at any time: a = b does exactly that.)

A reference and its referent have independent lifetimes: destroying a reference doesn’t affect the object (lifetime_reference_and_referent.cpp). The other way round is dangerous: if the object is destroyed first, the reference is left dangling, and using it is undefined behaviour. Finally, a reference is not an object, just a name; the compiler often gives it no memory at all. So far references look like a curiosity. Their real job comes next.

7.4 Pass by reference

Pass by value (Chapter 02) copies the argument into the parameter. That’s cheap for a double but not for a long std::string, and most standard library types are expensive to copy: in pass_by_value_string.cpp, every character is copied, used once and thrown away. Make the parameter a reference instead, void print_value(std::string& y), and it is simply bound to the argument. Nothing is copied.

The addresses prove it (&x gives the address of x, more in Chapter 08):

pass_by_value_vs_pass_by_reference.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print_addresses(double val, double& ref) {
    std::cout << "address of val (a copy):  " << &val << '\n';
    std::cout << "address of ref (no copy): " << &ref << '\n';
}

int main() {
    double x{42.0};
    std::cout << "address of x:             " << &x << '\n';
    print_addresses(x, x);
    return 0;
}

address of x:             0x7ffcc2285eb0
address of val (a copy):  0x7ffcc2285e98
address of ref (no copy): 0x7ffcc2285eb0

ref has the same address as x: it is x. Any change made through a non-const reference parameter therefore changes the caller’s argument, which is exactly what we need when a function’s purpose is to modify something. Remember the swap that didn’t swap in Chapter 02?

swap_by_reference.cpp
#include <iostream>

void swap_values(int& x, int& y) { // no copies
    int temp{x};
    x = y;
    y = temp;
}

int main() {
    int x{100};
    int y{200};
    swap_values(x, y);
    std::cout << "x = " << x << ", y = " << y << '\n';
    return 0;
}

x = 200, y = 100

7.4.1 Pass by const reference

A non-const reference parameter only accepts modifiable lvalues: print_value(z) with a const int z, or print_value(5), fails with the binding errors above (pass_by_reference_accept_modifiable_lvalues.cpp). But often we just want to read an expensive argument without copying it, whatever it is. A const reference binds to anything:

pass_by_const_reference.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print_value(const int& y) { // a const reference
    std::cout << y << '\n';
}

int main() {
    int x{5};
    print_value(x); // fine: a modifiable lvalue

    const int z{6};
    print_value(z); // fine: a const lvalue

    print_value(7); // fine: an rvalue (bound to a temporary)
    return 0;
}

5
6
7

That’s exactly why C++ lets const references bind to rvalues: otherwise you couldn’t pass a literal like 7 to a function taking a reference. And through a const reference, the function can’t change the argument (assignment of read-only reference). No copy and no accidental changes.

TipBest practice
  • Fundamental types (int, double, char, bool): pass by value. They’re cheap to copy.
  • Class types (std::string, std::vector, your own classes later): pass by const reference.
  • Pass by non-const reference only when the function is meant to change the argument.

For read-only text, C++17 also offers std::string_view, a cheap view of a string: the alternative Chapter 04 promised.

7.5 Return by reference

Returning by value copies the result back to the caller; returning a reference avoids that copy:

return_by_ref_academic.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

const std::string& get_program_name() { // returns a const reference
    // static: created once, lives until the program ends
    static const std::string program_name{"Calculator"};
    return program_name;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "This program is named " << get_program_name() << '\n';
    return 0;
}

This program is named Calculator

A static local variable is created once and lives until the program ends, unlike an ordinary local variable, and here that’s essential. Remove static, and program_name is destroyed when the function returns, so the caller receives a dangling reference (return_by_ref_lifetime.cpp):

$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall return_by_ref_lifetime.cpp
warning: reference to local variable 'program_name' returned
$ ./a.out
Segmentation fault

The object must outlive the function. That’s the case when a function returns a reference to one of the caller’s own objects:

return_by_ref_larger.cpp
#include <iostream>

int& larger(int& a, int& b) { // returns a reference to a or to b
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}

int main() {
    int x{5};
    int y{8};

    larger(x, y) = 0; // resets whichever is larger: here, y
    std::cout << "x = " << x << ", y = " << y << '\n';
    return 0;
}

x = 5, y = 0

larger() returns a reference to the caller’s y, so the call can even appear on the left of =: it’s an lvalue! This is safe because x and y outlive the call.

7.6 Summary

  • Every expression has a type and a value category. An lvalue is an identifiable object; an rvalue is just a value.
  • A reference (int& ref{x};) is another name for an existing object. It must be initialized and can’t be reseated.
  • A non-const reference binds only to modifiable lvalues; a const reference binds to anything.
  • Pass by reference avoids copies and lets a function change its argument; pass by const reference avoids copies without allowing changes. Pass fundamental types by value, class types by const reference.
  • Never return (or keep) a reference to an object that is about to be destroyed: dangling references are undefined behaviour.

Further reading on learncpp.com: value categories, pass by const lvalue reference, std::string_view, static local variables.

8 Pointers

A reference is a second name for an object. A pointer is another way to refer to an object: an object of its own, which holds the object’s address. This chapter introduces addresses, pointers, null and dangling pointers, and pass by address.

8.1 Memory and addresses

When int x{425}; runs, the program sets aside memory for x at some address, say 0x1234. Whenever we use x, the program reads or writes the value stored at that address, and a reference int& ref{x}; is just another name for the same memory. Two operators work with addresses. The address-of operator &x gives the address of x, and the dereference operator * does the opposite: given an address, it gives the object stored there.

dereference_operator_example.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    double x{5.0};
    std::cout << x << '\n';     // the value of x
    std::cout << &x << '\n';    // the address of x
    std::cout << *(&x) << '\n'; // the value AT that address
    return 0;
}

5
0x7ffcc49e7ee0
5

Addresses are usually printed in hexadecimal; yours will differ, and may change every run. An object bigger than one byte occupies several addresses, and & gives the first.

ImportantKey idea

& and * are opposites: & gets the address of an object, and * gets the object at an address. So *(&x) is just x.

The ampersand means different things in different places: after a type it declares a reference (int& ref{x};), before an expression it takes an address (&x), and between two expressions it’s bitwise AND (not covered here). The asterisk is similar: after a type it declares a pointer, before an expression it dereferences, and between two expressions it multiplies.

8.2 Pointers

A pointer is an object whose value is a memory address, usually the address of another object. double* is a pointer to a double: it holds the address of a double.

pointer_example.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int x{425};
    int* ptr{&x}; // ptr is a pointer to int, holding the address of x

    std::cout << "x lives at:   " << &x << '\n';
    std::cout << "ptr holds:    " << ptr << '\n';
    std::cout << "*ptr gives:   " << *ptr << '\n';
    std::cout << "ptr lives at: " << &ptr << '\n'; // a pointer is an object
    return 0;
}

x lives at:   0x7ffc45506a0c
ptr holds:    0x7ffc45506a0c
*ptr gives:   425
ptr lives at: 0x7ffc45506a10

ptr holds the address of x, so we say ptr points at x. *ptr is x itself, and ptr has an address of its own, because it’s an object.

The * in a declaration belongs to each variable, not to the type: int* ptr1, ptr2; makes ptr1 a pointer but ptr2 a plain int. Yet another reason to define one variable per line. An uninitialized pointer holds a garbage address and is called a wild pointer; dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. int* ptr{}; instead makes a null pointer, which points at nothing.

TipBest practice

Write the asterisk next to the type, int* ptr, as with references, and always initialize your pointers: with an address, or with nullptr.

8.2.1 Changing the pointer, or what it points at

pointer_assignment.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    double x{42.0};
    double y{24.0};
    double* ptr{&x}; // ptr points at x

    *ptr = 10.0; // changes x: x becomes 10
    std::cout << "x = " << x << '\n';

    ptr = &y;    // change what ptr points at: now y
    *ptr = 12.0; // so this changes y
    std::cout << "y = " << y << '\n';
    return 0;
}

x = 10
y = 12
ImportantKey idea

ptr = &y; assigns to the pointer: it now points somewhere else. *ptr = 12.0; assigns to the object pointed at.

8.2.2 Pointers versus references

A pointer can do much of what a reference does: in pointers_behave_like_references.cpp, changing x through ref or through *ptr changes the same object. But they are not the same thing:

References Pointers
must be initialized don’t have to be (but should be!)
are not objects are objects
can’t be reseated can be made to point somewhere else
always refer to an object can point at nothing (null)
“safe”, apart from dangling dangerous: wild, null and dangling pointers

&x doesn’t produce a bare number but a pointer: for an int x, &x has type int*, and double* dptr{&x}; fails with cannot convert ‘int*’ to ‘double*’. A pointer’s type says what kind of object lives at the address. Since a pointer is just an address, all pointers are the same size, whatever they point at: 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine (size_of_pointers.cpp).

8.3 Null and dangling pointers

null_pointer.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* ptr{nullptr}; // a null pointer: points at nothing

    if (ptr == nullptr) { // check before dereferencing!
        std::cout << "ptr is null\n";
    }

    int x{5};
    ptr = &x;
    if (ptr) { // a non-null pointer counts as true
        std::cout << "ptr points at " << *ptr << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

ptr is null
ptr points at 5

nullptr is a special value meaning “no address”, and a pointer holding it is a null pointer. A null pointer converts to false and any other pointer to true, so if (ptr) asks “does ptr point at something?”. There is no object at “no address”, so dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behaviour; on most systems the program crashes with a segmentation fault (null_dereference.cpp).

TipBest practice

If a pointer might be null, check it before you dereference it.

Like a dangling reference, a dangling pointer still holds the address of an object that has been destroyed:

dangling_pointer.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* ptr{nullptr};
    {
        int x{5};
        ptr = &x;
    } // x is destroyed here: ptr now dangles

    std::cout << *ptr << '\n'; // undefined behaviour!
    return 0;
}

$ g++ -Wall dangling_pointer.cpp
warning: using dangling pointer 'ptr' to 'x'
$ ./a.out
5

It printed 5 here, but with -O2 the same code printed 0: undefined behaviour, so anything can happen. Thank you, -Wall!

8.4 Pass by address

A function can take a pointer parameter, and the caller then passes an address:

pass_by_address.cpp
#include <iostream>

void print_value(const int* ptr) { // receives an address
    if (ptr == nullptr) {
        std::cout << "(no object)\n";
        return;
    }
    std::cout << *ptr << '\n';
}

int main() {
    int x{42};
    print_value(&x);      // pass the address of x
    print_value(nullptr); // "no object" is a valid argument
    return 0;
}

42
(no object)

const int* is a pointer to a const int: the function may read *ptr but not change it. With a plain int*, it could change the caller’s x through *ptr. Pass by address can do what pass by reference does, avoiding copies and changing the caller’s object, and the one extra thing it can do is mean “no object at all”, with nullptr. (The “proof” that scope is not lifetime in Chapter 02 was pass by address.)

TipBest practice

Prefer pass by (const) reference. Use pass by address only when “no object” is a valid argument.

Pointers really earn their place when a program creates objects while it runs, in the next chapter, and when we work with class hierarchies in Section 03.

8.5 Summary

  • Every object lives at an address. &x gives the address of x; *ptr gives the object at the address in ptr.
  • A pointer (int* ptr{&x};) is an object that holds an address. Assign to ptr to point elsewhere; assign to *ptr to change the object pointed at.
  • Always initialize pointers. nullptr means “points at nothing”; check before dereferencing.
  • Wild, null and dangling pointers lead to undefined behaviour when dereferenced.
  • References are safer, so prefer them. Use a pointer when “no object” must be possible.

Further reading on learncpp.com: null pointers, pointers and const, pass by address, C-style arrays.

9 Dynamic Memory Allocation

So far, every object got its memory automatically. This chapter creates objects while the program runs, on the heap, where pointers become essential, and where you are responsible for giving the memory back.

9.1 Why dynamic memory?

C++ gives memory to objects in three ways:

Allocation For Memory is obtained… …and given back
Static global and static variables once, when the program starts when the program ends
Automatic local variables, parameters when the block is entered automatically, at its }
Dynamic whatever you ask for when you ask, with new when you say, with delete

With static and automatic allocation, memory is obtained and given back automatically, and the size of every object must be known when the program is compiled. Usually that’s what we want, but not always. Often we only find out how much data there is when the program runs: how many measurements are in the file, how many particles are in the simulation. Guessing a maximum wastes memory when there are fewer and breaks when there are more. And local variables live in a region of memory called the stack, which is small: typically 1 MB (Windows) to 8 MB (Linux).

stack_overflow.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int numbers[10'000'000]; // 10 million ints (40 MB) on the stack
    numbers[0] = 1;
    std::cout << numbers[0] << '\n';
    return 0;
}

$ ./stack_overflow
Segmentation fault

int numbers[10'000'000]; is a C-style array of ten million ints. At 40 MB, it doesn’t fit on an 8 MB stack: a stack overflow, and the program crashes.

Dynamic memory allocation lets a running program ask for memory whenever it likes, as much as it needs. That memory comes from a much bigger region called the heap (or free store): gigabytes on a modern machine. Heap objects have no names, only addresses, and that’s what pointers are for.

9.2 new and delete

new_single.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* ptr{new int}; // an int on the heap
    *ptr = 7;          // use it through the pointer
    std::cout << *ptr << '\n';

    int* ptr2{new int{6}}; // allocate AND initialize
    std::cout << *ptr2 << '\n';

    delete ptr; // give the memory back
    delete ptr2;
    return 0;
}

7
6

new int creates an int on the heap and returns its address, an int*, which we must keep in a pointer, or the object is lost. new int{6} creates it and initializes it. When you’re done with a heap object, you must give its memory back with delete ptr;. Despite its name, delete doesn’t delete the pointer: ptr is an ordinary local variable and lives on. It destroys the object pointed at and hands the memory back. Only delete what came from new.

ImportantKey idea

Local variables are freed automatically. Heap objects are not: every new needs exactly one matching delete.

After delete, ptr still holds the old address: it’s a dangling pointer (Chapter 08).

use_after_delete.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* ptr{new int{7}};
    delete ptr; // ptr is now dangling

    std::cout << *ptr << '\n'; // undefined behaviour: use after delete
    delete ptr;                // undefined behaviour: delete twice
    return 0;
}

$ ./use_after_delete
1573893628
free(): double free detected in tcache 2
Aborted

Reading through the dangling pointer printed garbage, and deleting it again crashed the program: both are undefined behaviour. So after delete, set the pointer to nullptr, which also makes a handy “nothing allocated yet” marker. delete on a null pointer does nothing, so there’s no need to write if (ptr) delete ptr; (delete_and_nullptr.cpp).

TipBest practice

After delete, set the pointer to nullptr, unless it’s about to go out of scope anyway.

Dangling pointers are easy to create without noticing, when two pointers hold the same address:

int* owner{new int{5}};
int* viewer{owner}; // two pointers to the same heap int

delete owner;       // the int is gone...
owner = nullptr;    // ...and owner says so

// ...but viewer still holds the old address: it dangles!
TipBest practice

Avoid having several pointers to the same heap object. If you must, be clear about which one owns it: the owner is the only one that deletes it.

9.3 Memory leaks

memory_leak.cpp
void do_something() {
    int* ptr{new int{42}}; // allocated...
} // ptr is destroyed: the int leaks

int main() {
    do_something();
    return 0;
}

The pointer ptr is a local variable, destroyed at the }, but the heap int is not. Nobody holds its address any more, so nobody can ever delete it: a memory leak. A leaked object stays allocated until the program ends, and the operating system can’t reuse that memory either. One leaked int is harmless, but a leak inside a loop that runs a million times, in a simulation that runs for a week, eats all the memory and slows the whole machine down. And leaks make no noise: the program still “works”.

NoteComing from Python

Python has a garbage collector that frees objects nobody refers to any more. C++ has none: if you new it, you delete it. (Or let something else do it for you: the end of this chapter.)

You need a tool to find leaks. g++ can build your program with AddressSanitizer, a checker for memory bugs:

$ g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address memory_leak.cpp
$ ./a.out
==6651==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
Direct leak of 4 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
    #1 in do_something() memory_leak.cpp:2
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 4 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s).

It even names the line that allocated the leaked memory (the real report is longer). It catches dangling pointers too: on use_after_delete.cpp it reports heap-use-after-free on line 7.

TipBest practice

While developing, compile with -g -fsanitize=address now and then: it’s free bug-hunting. (It works on Linux and macOS; on Windows, MSVC has its own version.)

Besides a pointer going out of scope, there are two more common ways to leak. Reassigning the pointer, as in ptr = &value;, loses the heap object it pointed at, and so does allocating twice, as in ptr = new int{}; when ptr already holds an allocation. The fix for both is to delete before you reassign.

9.4 Dynamic arrays

new can also allocate a whole array, whose length can be any value known at run time: exactly what automatic memory couldn’t do.

dynamic_array.cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "How many numbers? ";
    int length{};
    std::cin >> length; // known only when the program runs

    int* numbers{new int[length]{}}; // length ints, all set to 0

    for (int i{0}; i < length; ++i) {
        numbers[i] = i * i; // the i-th int
    }
    for (int i{0}; i < length; ++i) {
        std::cout << numbers[i] << ' ';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';

    delete[] numbers; // array new needs array delete
    return 0;
}

$ ./dynamic_array
How many numbers? 6
0 1 4 9 16 25

new int[length] gives one block of length ints side by side, and a pointer to the first. numbers[i] is the int at position i, counting from 0 as with std::string. There’s no checking: numbers[length] is out of bounds, and undefined behaviour. new int[5]{} sets all the elements to 0, and new int[5]{9, 7, 5, 3, 1} gives them values.

Memory from new[] must be returned with delete[], and memory from new with plain delete. Mixing them up is undefined behaviour, yet it compiles: only -Wall warns (called on pointer returned from a mismatched allocation function, delete_mismatch.cpp), and AddressSanitizer reports an alloc-dealloc-mismatch.

Finally, new can fail if the memory isn’t available. It then throws an exception, std::bad_alloc, and the program stops (exceptions are beyond this course); new (std::nothrow) returns nullptr instead, so that you can check (new_can_fail.cpp). For everyday sizes, failure is rare.

9.5 Let someone else delete

Here is the dynamic array program again, with std::vector, which you’ve used in the labs:

vector_instead.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::cout << "How many numbers? ";
    int length{};
    std::cin >> length;

    std::vector<int> numbers(length);

    for (int i{0}; i < length; ++i) {
        numbers[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i{0}; i < length; ++i) {
        std::cout << numbers[i] << ' ';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
    return 0;
} // no delete[]: the vector frees its own memory here

Inside, std::vector does exactly what we did by hand: new[] to get memory, and delete[] when the vector is destroyed. You can’t forget the delete[], because you never write it. Note the parentheses on line 9: numbers(length) makes length zeros, whereas numbers{length} would hold the single value length.

For a single heap object, use a smart pointer:

unique_ptr_example.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory> // for std::unique_ptr and std::make_unique

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<int> ptr{std::make_unique<int>(42)};
    std::cout << *ptr << '\n'; // use it just like a pointer
    return 0;
} // no delete: the int is freed automatically here

A std::unique_ptr owns one heap object and deletes it automatically when it goes out of scope: no leaks, no forgotten delete. std::make_unique<int>(42) does the new for you. How can an object clean up after itself? With a destructor, a special function that runs when an object is destroyed; we write our own in Chapter 12.

TipBest practice

In your own code, prefer std::vector for dynamic arrays and std::unique_ptr (with std::make_unique) for single heap objects. Write new and delete by hand only when you have a good reason.

You still need to understand new and delete, though: they’re what std::vector, std::string and smart pointers do under the hood, you’ll meet them in older code and libraries and when we write classes that manage memory (Chapter 12), and they make clear what “owning” an object means, an idea that runs through all of modern C++.

9.6 Summary

  • Local variables live on the small stack and are freed automatically. Dynamic objects live on the large heap, and you manage them.
  • new creates an object on the heap and returns its address; delete gives the memory back. Every new needs exactly one delete.
  • After delete, the pointer dangles: set it to nullptr. Deleting nullptr is safe.
  • Losing the last pointer to a heap object is a memory leak. Find leaks with -fsanitize=address.
  • new int[n] makes an array whose length is known only at run time; free it with delete[], never plain delete.
  • In practice, let std::vector and std::unique_ptr do the deleting for you.

Further reading on learncpp.com: new and delete, dynamically allocating arrays, std::vector, std::unique_ptr.

That’s the end of Section 02. Section 03, Object-Oriented Programming, starts with Chapter 10.
